claims.text: Formation of a single-phase solid solution in noble metal–based high-entropy alloy nanoparticles is governed by competition between elemental reduction and nucleation kinetics.
Under rapid heating, the fastest-reducing noble metal ions nucleate first.
Early nuclei formed by fast-reducing metals act as seed sites that promote epitaxial growth.
Early seed formation causes preferential incorporation of some elements and limits incorporation of slower-reducing elements.
Preferential incorporation can trap nonequilibrium phases and produce phase separation and elemental segregation.
A slower thermal ramp or intermediate-temperature hold will make reduction of the constituent metals more uniform.
A slower thermal ramp will provide greater atomic or surface diffusion than rapid heating and cooling.
More balanced reduction and adequate surface diffusion facilitate uniform elemental mixing at nucleation sites.
Uniform elemental mixing stabilizes the target single-phase solid solution.
Relative to rapid heating and cooling, a slower thermal ramp will yield a more homogeneous elemental distribution.
Relative to rapid heating and cooling, a slower thermal ramp will yield a more consistent single-phase crystal structure.
Relative to rapid heating and cooling, a slower thermal ramp will yield more controlled nanoparticle morphology.
Rapid-heating and rapid-cooling synthesis often produces phase separation, elemental segregation, variable morphology, and uncontrolled crystal structure.
The proposed mechanism applies when synthesis kinetics dominate over thermodynamic equilibration.
The proposed mechanism is particularly applicable when constituent metals differ significantly in reduction behavior and atomic diffusion rates.
The proposed mechanism may not apply when all constituent metals have nearly identical reduction behaviors.
The controlled comparison should hold overall composition, atmosphere, and precursor concentration constant while changing the thermal ramp.
